{{nihongo|'''Fukuchi Shrine'''|富知神社}} is a [[shinto shrine]] in the [[Engishiki Jinmyōchō]]. It is located in [[Suruga Province]].

[[File:Fukuchi-jinja torii.JPG|thumb|200px|right|Torii]]
'''Fukuchi Shrine''' (???????) is a {{ill|Shinto shrine|Q845945|qid=Q845945}} in {{ill|Shizuoka Prefecture|Q131320|qid=Q131320}}{{ill|Fujinomiya, Shizuoka|Q496072|qid=Q496072}}. It is an Engishiki-listed {{ill|Shikinai Ronsha|Q135022904|qid=Q135022904}}, and a former sessha of {{ill|Fujisan Hongū Sengen Taisha|Q653180|qid=Q653180}}.

It is also known as "Fukuchi-sha," "Fukuchi My?jin-sha," "Fuji Shrine," and "Tomi Shrine"<ref name="??">"Place Names of Shizuoka Prefecture," entry for Fukuchi Shrine.</ref>.

=== Enshrined deity ===
* '''{{ill|Ōyamatsumi|Q386563|qid=Q386563|lt=?yamatsumi-no-Kami}}''' (also called ?yamazumi-no-Mikoto)<ref>The shrine history text writes "?yamatsumi-no-Kami," while the precinct sign writes "?yamazumi-no-Mikoto."</ref>
*: Father deity of {{ill|Konohanasakuya-hime|Q1781862|qid=Q1781862|lt=Konohanasakuya-hime-no-Mikoto}} (deity of Sengen Taisha).

=== History ===
=== Founding ===
Tradition says the shrine was founded in year 2 of {{ill|Emperor Kōshō|Q312841|qid=Q312841}} (Imperial era 187)<ref>It is said this is recorded in the ''Suruga Fudoki'' ("History of Sengen Shrine," chapter 11, section on sessha and massha).</ref>.

An Edo-period shrine tradition of Sengen Taisha (''Fuji Hong? Sengen Shaki'') states: "The site of the ?miya shrine was formerly the site of Fukuchi My?jin; Sengen Shrine was moved there. Fukuchi My?jin is the Engishiki-listed Fukuchi Shrine enshrining ?yamazumi-no-Mikoto." It says Fukuchi Shrine was the land guardian at the present Sengen Taisha site until Sengen Taisha moved there from Yamamiya (present {{ill|Yamamiya Sengen Shrine|Q11467749|qid=Q11467749}}) in Daid? 1 ({{ill|806|Q30021|qid=Q30021}}). With that move, Fukuchi Shrine relocated to its current place, but has remained deeply connected to Sengen Taisha rituals as the local guardian deity.

In {{ill|Hirata Atsutane|Q2572749|qid=Q2572749}}'s ''{{ill|Koshiden|Q11410975|qid=Q11410975}}'', it is written that this shrine existed in ?miya-ch? and was called Fukuchi Gongen.

=== Overview ===
In the mid-Heian ''{{ill|Engishiki|Q1342448|qid=Q1342448}}'' {{ill|Engishiki Jinmyōchō|Q11064932|qid=Q11064932}}, "Fukuchi Shrine" is listed in Fuji District, Suruga Province, and this shrine is treated as one of its candidate shrines. Another candidate is {{ill|UNKNOWN|lt=Fukuchi Rokusho Asama Shrine}} (Asama Honch?, {{ill|Fuji, Shizuoka|Q328613|qid=Q328613}}). The reading in the register is marked as "Fuji."

In the ''Suruga no kuni Jinmeich?,'' "Fukuchi Tenjin" appears at Senior Fifth Rank, Lower and "Fukuchi Chigi" at Junior Fifth Rank, Upper<ref>From shrine history text. See [{{NDLDC|991014/456}} Jinja Kakuroku, first volume] (National Diet Library Digital Collection), frames 456-457.</ref>.

An article in ''{{ill|Azuma Kagami|Q1042324|qid=Q1042324}}'' for Bunji 2 ({{ill|1186|Q19730|qid=Q19730}}) contains "Fukuchi-sha of Kamimandokoro in Fuji territory." Since "Fuji territory" is considered Sengen Taisha estate, this suggests it was under Sengen Taisha influence by then<ref name="??"/>.

Afterward, the shrine continued as a sessha of Sengen Taisha, and rituals were managed by the shrine official Fukuchi Day? of Sengen Taisha<ref name="??"/>. Since the appointment of Yamada Jinzabur? in Genki 3 ({{ill|1572|Q6670|qid=Q6670}}), the Yamada family is thought to have inherited the role of Fukuchi Day? until Meiji<ref name="??"/>.

It is confirmed as a sessha of Sengen Taisha until around Meiji, but is now effectively independent<ref>"History of Sengen Shrine," chapter 11, section on sessha and massha.</ref>.

=== Annual festival ===
The annual festival day is September 19. The festival is now run by a rotating duty among four parish groups (Fuku, Kanga, Kandate, and Hagoromo). Since Reiwa 1, a parish youth association has organized children's mikoshi processions in thanks to the shrine deity and for community prosperity. From Reiwa 4 onward, the annual festival has been held on the weekend nearest September 19 in line with that procession.
[[????:???????.jpg|?????|{{ill|UNKNOWN|lt=Shink?sai}}]]
Reiwa 2 duty: Fuku district - {{ill|Tegomai|Q11496936|qid=Q11496936}}, shrine-name banner, drums, children's {{ill|Mikoshi|Q979940|qid=Q979940}}.

Reiwa 3 duty: Fuku district - shrine-name banner, drums, children's mikoshi.

Reiwa 4 duty: Kanga district - {{ill|UNKNOWN|lt=takahari}}, tekomai, shrine-name banner, drums, children's mikoshi.

Reiwa 5 duty: Kandate district - takahari, tekomai, shrine-name banner, drums, children's mikoshi.

Reiwa 6 duty: Hagoromo district - takahari, tekomai, shrine-name banner, drums, takahari, {{ill|Hayashi (music)|Q4171186|qid=Q4171186}} troupe, children's mikoshi, main shrine mikoshi.

== Considerations ==
[[File:Wakutama-ike-2.JPG|thumb|200px|right|{{ill|Wakutamaike|Q11563392|qid=Q11563392}} (within Sengen Taisha precincts)]]
Regarding "Fukuchi" in the shrine name, a relation to the name of Mt. Fuji has been pointed out. Historical documents preserve two old-name systems for Mt. Fuji<ref name="?????">"Nihon no Kamigami," entry for Fujisan Hong? Sengen Taisha.</ref>:
* Fushi-type: ?? / ?? (''{{ill|Man'yōshū|Q834321|qid=Q834321}}''), ?? (''{{ill|Hitachi no Kuni Fudoki|Q11481687|qid=Q11481687}}'')
* Fuchi-type: ?? (this shrine), ?? (''{{ill|UNKNOWN|lt=Wamy?sh?}}'', Tsuru District, Kai Province)

The "Fuchi" old name is said to derive from water worship<ref name="?????"/>. In ''Fuji Hong? Sengen Shaki,'' this shrine is said to have originally stood at the current Sengen Taisha site, where spring water emerges at {{ill|Wakutamaike|Q11563392|qid=Q11563392}}; worship there likely centered on that spring as "wakutama" (gushing sacred spirit)<ref name="?????"/>.

By contrast, the old name "Asama" for the Sengen deity is considered a word for "volcano," as seen in {{ill|Mount Aso|Q733710|qid=Q733710}}, {{ill|Mount Asama|ar|جبل أساما|arz|جبل اساما|az|Asama dağı|be|Асама|be_x_old|Асама|ca|Mont Asama|ceb|Asama-yama (bukid sa Hapon)|ckb|چیای ئاساما|cs|Asama (sopka)|de|Asama|es|Monte Asama|et|Asama|fa|کوه آساما|fi|Asama|fr|Mont Asama|he|הר אסאמה|id|Gunung Asama|it|Monte Asama|ja|浅間山|jv|Gunung Asama|ka|ასამა|kk|Асама|ko|아사마산|lt|Asama|min|Gunuang Asama|mk|Асама|ml|അസാമാ പർവ്വതം|mr|माउंट असामा|my|အဆမတောင်|nl|Asama (vulkaan)|no|Asama|oc|Asama (volcan)|pl|Asama|pnb|ٹلہ اسامہ|pt|Monte Asama|ro|Muntele Asama|ru|Асама|sco|Mount Asama|sk|Asama (sopka)|sq|Mali Asama|sv|Asama|th|เขาอาซามะ|tr|Asama Dağı|uk|Асама (гора)|uz|Asama|vi|Núi Asama|wuu|浅间山|zh|淺間山|zh_yue|淺間山|qid=Q242730}}, and {{ill|Mount Asahi|Q11517490|qid=Q11517490|lt=Asahidake}}<ref name="?????"/>. It is suggested that the need to pacify Fuji eruptions led fire-god worship to overtake water-god worship<ref name="?????"/>. The earliest record of Fuji eruption in official history appears in ''{{ill|Shoku Nihongi|Q611399|qid=Q611399}}'', Ten'? 1 ({{ill|781|Q31175|qid=Q31175}}), seventh month; earlier records describe Fuji only as a peaceful mountain, implying major eruptions had not yet occurred<ref name="?????"/>.

From this perspective, the ritual shift traditionally dated to Daid? 1 ({{ill|806|Q30021|qid=Q30021}}) is interpreted as symbolizing a transition from "water-deity worship (Fuchi)" to "fire-deity worship (Asama)" on Mt. Fuji<ref name="?????"/>.
